extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in academic misconduct/case studies
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia article documenting the career, investigations, findings, and consequences of a single researcher's scientific misconduct (Diederik Stapel). Useful as a case study of fabrication/manipulation in social‑psychology research and institutional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabrication of data
rubrics_metrics.description: Stapel fabricated data for research publications — i.e., he created fictitious data instead of collecting it (the article says he 'faked studies' and 'made up the data').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and explanation in the article: formulating full study elements (hypotheses, methods, stimuli, questionnaires, participants' rewards) and then creating fictitious datasets provided to colleagues and students; pretending experiments were run with unnamed research assistants; claiming access to schools that did not exist (the 'smoking gun'). The Levelt report identified many publications where fabrication was established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulation of data
rubrics_metrics.description: Altering recorded outcome measures or numerals in real datasets so calculated means support a tested hypothesis ('manipulated data').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earlier in his career Stapel appears to have manipulated data by altering numerals so that means for contrasted experimental conditions would appear to differ. This is contrasted with outright fabrication; both were treated as scientific misconduct by investigators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control and concealment of raw data / refusal of scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices that prevent independent access to or verification of raw data (e.g., controlling data files, giving excuses when students asked to see raw data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents that Stapel often controlled the data in his lab, returned data files to himself via an assistant, discouraged curiosity regarding datasets, and met persistent questioning with hostility. Such concealment impeded detection and was highlighted by investigation committees as improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspicious data patterns and 'too good to be true' results
rubrics_metrics.description: Data that fit hypotheses implausibly well or show anomalous patterns (e.g., identical rows repeated across studies), triggering suspicion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whistleblowers noticed anomalous data: an entire row of scores appearing identically in two studies and data fitting the hypothesis so perfectly that colleagues joked 'It is as if he made up these data himself.' The Levelt committee and other researchers flagged 'too good to be true' results as an indicator of possible fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fabricated participants/contacts (bogus data sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming data were collected by contacts or in institutions that do not exist, or fabricating access to participant pools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pressed for contact details of schools where data were allegedly collected, Stapel admitted the schools did not exist — identified in the article as the 'smoking gun'. Fabricated participant sources are an explicit form of evidence for fabrication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Providing pre‑collected data to students instead of involving them in collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplying graduate students with pre‑collected datasets rather than having them conduct experiments themselves, an atypical practice for masters/PhD training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes Stapel's supply of pre‑collected data was presented as an advantage but was atypical; many students graduated without actually completing experiments. Investigators regarded this process as inappropriate and harmful to students' training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuse of supervisory power and pressure to silence questioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Using authority to discourage or punish scrutiny by students and junior researchers (hostility, pressure to 'just write up the results').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: PhD students reporting being pressured into silence; a student querying unusual data being told to 'just write up the results' to be taken on. Committees concluded Stapel used power to suppress dissent, causing severe damage to young researchers' careers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional investigation procedures and evidence review
rubrics_metrics.description: Formation of investigative committees, interim and final reports, systematic analysis of publications, public reporting of findings and creation of investigation websites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Levelt, Noort and Drenth committees were formed to investigate Stapel's work; they analyzed 130 articles and 24 book chapters, published interim and final reports, set up a website for interim findings, and used staged review procedures to classify and report evidence of misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of findings / levels of certainty (e.g., 'fraud established' vs 'evidence of fraud' vs 'suspect')
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative reports distinguish degrees of certainty about publications (e.g., 'fraud established', 'evidence of fraud', 'suspect') and act accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes that some chapters/publications were labeled 'fraud established' whereas others had only 'evidence of fraud' or were 'suspect' (e.g., Noort committee's less certain conclusions where original data were scarce). The committees used such classifications to recommend actions like retractions or further inquiry and advised on whether students' degrees should be retracted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction of publications and publisher actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals and book publishers retract or excise material once fabrication/manipulation is found (formal retraction notices, removal of chapters from later editions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Science retracted a co‑authored paper after the university's findings; publishers republished an edited volume with Stapel's chapter excised; Retraction Watch tracked 58 retracted publications for Stapel as of 2015. Retraction statements often note coauthors were not involved in data generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences, sanctions, and settlements
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional and legal consequences for misconduct, including suspension, surrendering titles, criminal prosecution or settlement (community service, loss of benefits), and retraction of awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stapel was suspended, voluntarily surrendered his PhD title, faced potential prosecution but settled (120 hours community service and loss of some benefits), and had awards retracted. The article notes prosecutors took his voluntary surrender into account when deciding not to pursue criminal actions further.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of coauthors' and students' involvement and protection of degrees
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluating whether coauthors or students were aware of misconduct and whether their degrees or reputations should be affected (e.g., not retracting students' degrees if unaware).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The committees emphasized that Stapel acted alone in known cases and found no indication coauthors or PhD students were aware; they advised degrees of students involved should not be retracted in many cases, though some theses were marked with varying degrees of suspicion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damage to scientific trust and recommendations for systemic change
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that individual misconduct can severely damage young researchers and public confidence in science, and that systemic academic responsibilities may be lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Levelt interim report stated Stapel had caused severe damage to young people and to general confidence in science, particularly social psychology; reviewers of Stapel's memoir and commentators used the case to discuss systemic failures and the myth of self‑correction in science.
